Markdown reads an HTML block where markdown-it does and draws it as Rich does, not at all (rich-unfiled-791c.e5pf)

CommonMark's seven HTML block kinds, matched as markdown-it matches them.
Every kind but a lone tag ends a paragraph, a table body and a lazy
continuation, through opensBlock. The block is kept as a token that draws
nothing, so a container ending in one does not read as ending in the
paragraph before it.

Markdown draws a GFM pipe table as Rich's Table (rich-demos-k78j.5yo) (#417)

* Markdown draws a GFM pipe table as Rich's Table (rich-demos-k78j.5yo)

A header row, then a delimiter row naming as many columns, is a table, read
as markdown-it reads one: tried before every other block, able to end a
paragraph, its body running to a blank line or a line that opens a block.
Each cell keeps its inline Markdown and sits where its delimiter's colons
put it; the header is drawn in markdown.table.header and the borders in
markdown.table.border, the styles and Table settings Rich uses.

Pinned against Rich 14's own output. Column widths are Table's, which
divides a squeezed width differently from Rich on purpose (table.ts
header), so a wide table wraps its cells at other columns than Rich's.

* A Markdown table is read as markdown-it reads one, capped as it caps (rich-demos-k78j.5yo)

Review of PR 417: the page and comments said GFM, but the parser is
markdown-it's, which tries a table before any other block where GitHub
does not. Body rows now stop at markdown-it's 65536 filled-out cells,
one predicate says which lines may be table rows, and a header row is
split only once its delimiter row is one.

Frames prepares its sequence once, not once a frame (rich-unfiled-791c.cxcp) (#418)

* Frames prepares its sequence once, not once a frame (rich-unfiled-791c.cxcp)

FrameSequence is the frames prepared once — beat, width, each frame set
into a line and padded — and Frames is that sequence at a t, finding only
the index. Spinner holds two prepared sequences and builds nothing per
frame. new Frames over 90 frames: 25.95 µs before, 0.12 µs after (0.13 µs
over 1 frame).

* Review: comments name FrameSequence where the split moved the work (rich-unfiled-791c.cxcp)

A spinner's next change and a Live's next frame are on the host's timeline

Review (high) on PR #416.

Spinner scaled t by speed before Frames, so its nextChange stamp was on
the scaled timeline: speed 2 said interval when the frame turns at half
that, and a negative speed said a time in the past. The holds are now
scaled instead — interval over |speed|, the frames reversed for a
negative one — so Frames stamps host time and nothing maps back. Speed 0
is refused: an infinite hold is not a beat. The negative-speed test had
pinned frame 0 at exactly t = 0, an instant-wide sliver of the old wrap.

Live armed the next wake from a second clock read after the paint, so the
rate stretched by what each frame cost to draw, and a change that fell
due during the paint was deferred a whole interval. The wake is now
measured from the frame's own t; Clock.at fires at once for a past time.

The option doc says the next frame is a frame interval after the last one
drawn, a manual refresh included; frameClock's header says at() wakes
nothing unless something runs every() on it.

Rejected with evidence: a stamp-only Style failing isNull on the SGR hot
path. Bench (120-col row, 600 frames at 1/60 s, truecolor), p50 ms
master → branch: shimmer 0.145 → 0.139, pulse 0.114 → 0.114, sparkle
0.309 → 0.179, wheel 0.112 → 0.110.

A host can ask when what it draws next changes (rich-animation-xi28.6rs)

Every animated primitive stamps its cells with the moment what they show
next changes, on `Style.nextChange`, which rides up through every container
as the anchor does and writes no byte. `Segment.nextChange` reads the
soonest off a composed frame: a `Frames` answers the next frame's start,
`Effected` what its effect says — a stepped signal and `onBeat` their next
step (`Beat.end`), a transition `t` until it is done and never after, a
plain loop `t` itself — and still content never, as `Infinity`.

`Effect` is now an interface: the call, and an optional `nextChange(t)`;
`withNextChange` attaches one, `nextChangeOf` is the one reading of an
absent one. `Clock.at(time, tick)` is the one-shot a host waits on, and
`Live` arms it after each frame — at the frame's next change or the rate's
next frame, whichever is sooner — so it draws each frame of a sequence held
shorter than its interval instead of a sample of them.

The showcase's brand carries a flash that declares its own schedule, and
its tagline counts down to the gauge's next step.
